client: I've been really struggling since I started college last semester. I feel like I can't keep up with any of my coursework, and it's gotten so bad that I've basically stopped hanging out with my friends altogether. I don't know if talking about it is actually going to change anything, but I figured I'd give this a shot.
therapist: It sounds like this past semester has been really overwhelming — feeling behind academically and pulling away from friends is a heavy combination to carry. I'm glad you decided to give this a shot, and I want you to know that even just putting words to what's been going on is a meaningful first step. What do you think has felt hardest to manage — the coursework itself, the isolation, or something else entirely?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: Honestly, I think the hardest part is the guilt that comes with the isolation — like, I know I've been pulling away from people, and then I feel terrible about it, but I also just can't bring myself to reach out. It's this loop I can't seem to break out of. The coursework is stressful too, but it's more like... the loneliness is what keeps me up at night.
therapist: That cycle you're describing — pulling away, then feeling guilty, which makes it even harder to reach out — is such a painful trap to be stuck in, and it makes a lot of sense that it's what's keeping you up at night. The loneliness and the guilt end up feeding each other, which can make the whole thing feel almost impossible to break. I'm curious — when you imagine reaching out to a friend, what's the thought or feeling that stops you in your tracks?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I think the first thing that hits me is this fear that they've already written me off, like I've been so absent that reaching out now would just be... weird or unwanted. And then there's this voice that says I don't deserve to just waltz back in after being so distant, that I should have to earn my way back somehow. It's almost easier to just stay withdrawn than to risk finding out that the friendship is already gone.
therapist: That voice telling you that you need to "earn your way back" is such a telling one — it sounds like a belief that your friendships are conditional on you always showing up perfectly, which is a really painful standard to hold yourself to. It's worth gently questioning whether your friends actually see it that way, or if that's a story the fear is telling you to keep you feeling safe by staying withdrawn. What do you think a close friend would actually say if you reached out to them today?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I mean... I know logically that my friends probably wouldn't judge me for going quiet for a while. But there's this part of me that just keeps saying "you've been gone too long, it's too awkward now, you've already messed it up." And honestly, even imagining reaching out to someone today makes my chest tighten — like I already know it's going to go badly somehow, even though I can't actually predict that.
therapist: What you just described — knowing one thing logically but feeling something completely different in your body — is actually at the heart of what we often work with in CBT, and that chest tightening is your mind treating an imagined outcome as if it's already real. That automatic prediction that "it's going to go badly" is worth slowing down and examining, because it's driving a lot of your avoidance even though it's just a thought, not a fact. If you were to actually test that prediction by reaching out to one person, what's the smallest, lowest-stakes version of that you could imagine?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and I get the logic of it, but even thinking about "the smallest version" of reaching out to someone makes my stomach drop. Like, who would I even contact? Most of the people I used to be close to have kind of drifted away, and I feel like so much time has passed that reaching out now would just be awkward or weird. It's not that I don't want connection, it's that I genuinely don't know if there's anyone left who would actually want to hear from me.
therapist: The way you're describing this — the stomach drop, not even knowing who to reach out to — really speaks to how deep the isolation has gone, and that question of "is there anyone left who would want to hear from me" sounds less like a fact and more like loneliness talking. It's a painful place to be, but I want to gently reflect back that you came here today and opened up, which tells me the part of you that wants connection is still very much alive. Can you think of even one person from before — not necessarily someone you were closest to, but someone who gave you a good feeling — who might still be out there?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I appreciate what you're saying, and yeah, maybe it is loneliness talking... but it's hard to separate that from reality when it's been so long. There's this one guy, Marcus, we used to grab coffee sometimes back when I was at my old job, and he always seemed genuinely happy to see me. But that was like three years ago, and I just keep thinking — why would he even remember me, let alone want to hear from some person who basically disappeared?
therapist: The fact that Marcus came to mind so readily — and that you still remember he seemed *genuinely* happy to see you — suggests that connection meant something real, even if time has passed. Three years might feel like a long time to you, but people often remember warmth more than they remember absence. What do you think Marcus would actually say if he got a message from you today?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I want to say he'd be happy to hear from me, but honestly my brain immediately goes to the worst case — like, what if he's moved on and has a whole new group of friends and doesn't even really remember me that well? It's easier to just not reach out than to find out that the connection I remember meant more to me than it did to him. That gap between what I hope and what might actually be true feels really uncomfortable to sit with.
therapist: That gap you're describing — between what you hope and what might be true — is such a vulnerable place to sit, and it makes sense that avoidance feels safer than risking disappointment. But I notice that even as you're describing the worst case, there's a part of you that *wants* to say he'd be happy to hear from you — and that hope is worth paying attention to. What would it mean for you if you reached out and it actually went well?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I mean... if it actually went well, I think I'd feel relieved more than anything. Like maybe I haven't completely destroyed that friendship just by pulling away for so long. But honestly, even imagining it going well feels kind of dangerous, because then I'd have to sit with how much I've missed him and how guilty I feel for letting so much time pass.
therapist: It's really meaningful that you can already feel what relief might be like — that tells me part of you genuinely believes the friendship could still be there. And what you said about imagining it going well feeling "dangerous" is so honest, because hope can feel like a risk when you've been protecting yourself from disappointment for so long. I'm wondering if the guilt you're anticipating is actually part of what's been keeping you stuck — like you might need to forgive yourself a little before you can let yourself reach back out?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: That thing you said about needing to forgive myself first... I don't know, it kind of landed differently than I expected. Like, I've been so focused on whether she would forgive me for pulling away that I haven't really thought about whether I've been holding something against myself this whole time. But honestly, I'm not even sure I know how to do that — forgiving myself feels kind of abstract, like you're telling me to just decide to feel differently, and I don't think it works that way for me.
therapist: You're absolutely right that self-forgiveness isn't just a decision you make — it's more of a process, and it often starts with something much smaller, like simply acknowledging that you were struggling and did what you could to cope, even if it wasn't perfect. I also noticed you shifted from "him" to "her" just now — is there someone else on your mind, maybe someone the guilt feels even heavier with?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: Yeah, I noticed that slip too... I think I was actually thinking about my sister. The guilt with her feels different — heavier, maybe, because she's still in my life and I still have to face her, unlike with him where I can just... avoid the whole thing. It's like with her, there's no clean ending, no way to just close the door and move on.
therapist: The way you're describing your sister — that there's no door to close, no way to avoid it — sounds like it carries a particular kind of weight that's different from the friendships you mentioned. I notice as you said it, there was something almost quiet in how you shared that, like it's something you've been sitting with for a long time but maybe haven't said out loud very often. What does the guilt with her actually feel like — is it more about specific things that happened, or more about the distance itself?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech
